kf1.tip: Choose a dish you eat at home and say which of denaturation, coagulation, gluten formation and foam formation happen in it, naming the step that causes each.
kf1.note: A good answer names a real dish and links each property to the step that causes it. Denaturation comes from heat, acid or beating. Coagulation comes from continued heating that sets the protein. Gluten formation comes from kneading or mixing wheat flour with water. Foam formation comes from whisking egg whites. Only claim what your dish really has. If you list a property without its step, or claim gluten with no wheat flour, the answer falls short.

kf2.tip: Imagine a béchamel sauce is heated only to 65°C instead of 85°C. Say what happens to the starch granules and how thick the sauce ends up.
kf2.note: The granules absorb the milk and swell, because the sauce is above 60°C. But they do not burst, because that happens around 85°C. So the starch molecules are never released to tangle together, and the sauce stays thin instead of thickening properly. If you said it thickens fully, check the two temperatures again. Swelling starts the process, but bursting is what thickens the sauce.

cs1.tip: Explain the difference between denaturation and coagulation to a Year 7, using your own everyday comparison instead of 'unravel, then re-join'.
cs1.note: A strong answer keeps the order right. Denaturation comes first: heat, acid, salt or beating breaks the bonds, and each coiled protein unfolds into a loose chain but stays a separate molecule. Coagulation follows: those loose chains bond to each other and set into a solid. Your comparison should show two distinct steps, something coming apart and then joining up. If your comparison has only one step, or both happen at once, it repeats the misconception.
